prompt: Whose book of 1981 is the best-known source of the cost-of-defect curve?

choices.text: Edsger Dijkstra
choices.why: Dijkstra’s sentence is about presence and absence.

choices.text: Barry Boehm
choices.why: Right: data from large projects of the 1970s.

choices.text: Laurent Bossavit, who studied where the chart came from
choices.why: Bossavit is the critic who traced the citations.

choices.text: Larry Smith
choices.why: He coined "shift left", in 2001.

prompt: In Boehm and Basili’s list of 2001, what ratio did they give for small, non-critical systems?

choices.text: Around 1000 to 1, because they ship more often
choices.why: Shipping often flattens the curve, if anything.

choices.text: About 5 to 1
choices.why: Right: against "often 100" for the large ones.

choices.text: Often 100 to 1, the same as for large systems
choices.why: That is the large, critical case.

choices.text: 1 to 1: no difference at all
choices.why: The paper still found late fixes dearer; less so.

prompt: What did Laurent Bossavit find when he traced the chart back to its sources?

choices.text: A large modern study confirming 100 to 1
choices.why: Later studies of short-cycle projects found flatter curves.

choices.text: That the curve runs the other way
choices.why: Nothing says a late defect is cheaper.

choices.text: Proof that Boehm made his data up
choices.why: Boehm’s data was real; the trouble is how it was copied and generalised.

choices.text: A chain of citations whose numbers drifted, some with no data behind them
choices.why: Right: a book quoting a paper quoting a talk.

prompt: A manager who ships every day says "the hundred-times rule is nonsense here". What is the strongest reply this lesson gives you?

choices.text: Argue from what this defect would cost if it shipped
choices.why: Right: the ratio depends on the project; refunds and Célia’s evening do not need one.

choices.text: Quote Boehm’s 1981 book
choices.why: That invites a debate about a chart, and on his project the manager may be right.

choices.text: Say testing should then stop
choices.why: A flatter curve does not mean defects are free.

choices.text: Show the curve again, in log scale
choices.why: Same chart, same debate.

prompt: Match each thing that grows to an example of it at Cine Aurora.

pairs.right: the seat map built on a wrong idea of a reservation
a pensioner refunded at the counter
Rafael, six months after writing the line
report, triage, fix, review, retest, release

prompt: Why do defects in requirements and design grow fastest?

choices.text: They are harder to see in a running program than a wrong price is
choices.why: Visibility is a separate matter; growth comes from what depends on them.

choices.text: Because testers are not allowed to read requirements
choices.why: Reading requirements is exactly what prevents them.

choices.text: Requirements change every week
choices.why: Change rate is not the mechanism named.

choices.text: Everything after them is built on top
choices.why: Right: the defect does not grow, its dependants do.

prompt: Which of the four costs can be cut without finding any defect earlier?
hint: Tests and requirements kept beside the code.

choices.text: None of them
choices.why: One of them can.

choices.text: The lost context
choices.why: Right: tests that say what the code is for are context that does not decay.

choices.text: What has been built on top of the defect by the time it is found
choices.why: That only shrinks if the defect is found sooner.

choices.text: Who has met it
choices.why: Only finding it before release keeps that to the team.

prompt: Before release, a defect is a technical problem. What does the lesson say it becomes after release?

choices.text: The customer’s problem, no longer the team’s
choices.why: It is very much the team’s, with more people involved.

choices.text: Nothing different
choices.why: Refunds and conversations are new costs.

choices.text: A commercial problem, and in some domains a legal one
choices.why: Right: the fix in the code is the same; everything around it is not.

choices.text: A bigger technical problem, since the code fix is harder after release
choices.why: The fix may be the same character; the cost moved elsewhere.

prompt: How many tickets did `overcharge.py` find sold to a sixty-year-old outside a Wednesday?
hint: The second line of its output.

prompt: How many reais did `overcharge.py` find charged too much in the month?

hint: What does everybody pay on a Wednesday?

choices.text: The cinema is closed on Wednesdays
choices.why: Wednesday is the half-price day, not a closed one.

choices.text: `tickets.py` crashes for "wed"
choices.why: It prints a price for Wednesday; lesson 1 ran one.

choices.text: Sales on Wednesdays are generated without a seed and change every run
choices.why: One seed makes the whole month.

choices.text: Everyone pays half then, so a sixty-year-old loses nothing
choices.why: Right: the Wednesday rule masks the defect that day.

prompt: The count says R$ 658,00. Why does the lesson call that number the floor of the cost?
hint: What is not in the output?

choices.text: It is the lowest price a ticket can have
choices.why: It is a total, not a price.

choices.text: Everything it does not count comes on top
choices.why: Right: finding the customers, refund fees and Célia’s evenings are all extra.

choices.text: Because the sales are invented
choices.why: The prices are the shop’s own; the invented month is a plausible stand-in.

choices.text: Because the program contains an error
choices.why: The program counts correctly what it says it counts.

hint: Draw the lifecycle left to right.

choices.text: Removing the testing that used to happen at the end
choices.why: That is stopping detection, not shifting anything.

choices.text: Moving testers to another team
choices.why: It is about when, not where people sit.

choices.text: Testing in production
choices.why: That is shift right.

choices.text: Doing quality work earlier
choices.why: Right: reviewing requirements, testing as code is written.

prompt: Which of these is shift right rather than shift left?

choices.text: Writing a test before the code
choices.why: Left, and lesson 15.

choices.text: Asking "over 60, or 60 and over?"
choices.why: Prevention in a sentence: left.

choices.text: Releasing a change to a few customers first and watching what happens
choices.why: Right: it finds what only real use can show, quickly.

choices.text: Reviewing the requirement with the product owner before the sprint starts
choices.why: That is as far left as it goes.

prompt: A tester proposes three people review every requirement for an hour, including a one-line label change. What question does the lesson say to ask?

choices.text: Can it be found earlier?
choices.why: Almost always yes, so it decides nothing.

choices.text: Is the hundred-times rule true for labels?
choices.why: The ratio is not how to decide.

choices.text: Who is to blame for the label?
choices.why: Blame is lesson 18’s non-question.

choices.text: Is it worth finding this earlier?
choices.why: Right: a label has nothing built on it; a reservation model does.

prompt: Order these moments for finding the sixty-year-old’s defect from cheapest to dearest.
hint: Count what has grown at each.
trap: The order of the lifecycle and the order of cost coincide for this defect.

prompt: A misspelt word on the help page and a wrong rule for holding seats are both found a month after release. Which statement fits this lesson?
hint: The ratio depends on the defect.

choices.text: The seat rule cost far more for the wait
choices.why: Right: what grew depends on what was built on it and who met it.

choices.text: Both cost a hundred times more than if found in the requirement
choices.why: A fixed multiplier is exactly the claim the lesson questions.

choices.text: Neither matters once the month is over
choices.why: The seat rule has a month of reservations built on it.

choices.text: The typo cost more, because more people read the help page than reserve seats
choices.why: Being read is not the same as being harmed by it.
